title: UCC lien search for small business loans: what lenders need to know
summary: Learn how UCC lien searches help lenders find existing claims on business assets, assess repayment priority, and check collateral before funding a loan.
body_markdown:
#### **What is a UCC-1 financing statement?**


It is a public notice of a creditor’s claimed interest in specified business property. It helps other lenders identify potential claims, but it does not by itself prove that the debt remains unpaid or that the claim is enforceable.


#### **Where do you search for UCC filings?**


For a corporation or LLC, start with the designated filing office, usually the Secretary of State, in its state of formation. For example, a Delaware LLC with a California store generally has ordinary UCC filings in Delaware. For an individual borrower, including a sole proprietor, the general rule uses the person’s principal residence.[UCC Section 9-307](https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/9/9-307) defines these locations. Other business structures and certain assets, including some property attached to real estate, follow different rules.


#### **How long does a UCC lien remain active?**


A standard financing statement generally lasts five years. A creditor can extend it for another five years by filing a continuation statement within the six months before it expires, under[UCC Section 9-515](https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/9/9-515) . Some filings have different durations. An expired notice does not necessarily mean the debt has been repaid, so check the filing history and current loan information.


#### **Can a later filing take priority over an earlier one?**


Yes.[UCC Section 9-324](https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/9/9-324) gives certain loans used to buy assets priority over existing claims on those assets if the lender meets the applicable requirements. A lender can also agree to let another lender[take priority](https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/9/9-339) . Filing dates are a starting point, not a complete answer.


#### **Does a mistake in the borrower’s name invalidate a UCC filing?**


Not always. Under[UCC Section 9-506](https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/9/9-506) , a name error may not invalidate the filing if a search under the correct name using the filing office’s standard search method would still find it. A doing-business-as (DBA) name is the name a business trades under. Using only that name does not satisfy the debtor-name requirement.
